questions.question: What general rule does the chapter give for choosing an algorithm to solve a problem?
gold_points: We should prefer an algorithm that is easy to understand, implement, and document.
When performance matters, we must also consider speed and efficient use of computing resources.
Algorithm choice balances understandability with performance concerns.
gold_source: Section 3.1 What This Chapter Is About, PDF page 1 (book page 89)

questions.question: Why is simplicity important when choosing an algorithm for long-term use?
gold_points: A simple algorithm is easier to implement correctly than a complex one.
It is less likely to contain subtle bugs that appear later on unexpected inputs.
A simple algorithm is easier for other people to understand and maintain over time.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: How can good documentation help when an algorithm is not very simple?
gold_points: Good comments and documentation can partially compensate for a lack of simplicity.
Clear explanation makes the algorithm easier for a reasonably intelligent reader to understand.
Documentation helps later modification and maintenance by other programmers.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 3 (book page 91)

questions.question: Besides running time, what other resources may a program need to conserve?
gold_points: The amount of storage space used by variables.
The amount of traffic generated on a computer network.
The amount of data moved to and from disks.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: Why does the chapter treat running time as the main efficiency concern for large problems?
gold_points: For large problems, running time determines whether a program can practically be used.
Other resources can matter, but running time is the dominant concern in this chapter.
Program efficiency is taken mainly to mean time as a function of input size.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: Summarize why simplicity matters when choosing an algorithm using bullet points.
gold_points: A simple algorithm is easier to implement correctly.
It is less likely to hide subtle bugs that appear later on unusual inputs.
It is easier for other programmers to understand, document, and maintain over time.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: Explain to a beginner why a linear-time algorithm can beat a quadratic-time algorithm for large inputs.
gold_points: A quadratic algorithm may still look competitive on small inputs because of constant factors.
As the input grows, the slower growth rate of the linear algorithm becomes a bigger advantage.
For large problems, growth rate matters more than a small constant-speed benefit.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 6 (book page 94)

questions.question: List the other resources besides running time that a program may need to conserve.
gold_points: Storage space used by variables is one important resource.
Traffic generated on a computer network is another resource that may need to be conserved.
Data moved to and from disks is also treated as a resource concern.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: Explain in plain language why it is hard to predict the exact running time of a C program in seconds.
gold_points: Exact running time depends on the specific machine used.
It also depends on the compiler and the generated machine code.
Even when those are fixed, counting every executed instruction exactly is still often too complicated.
gold_source: Section 3.4 Big-Oh and Approximate Running Time, PDF page 8 (book page 96)

questions.question: Explain why O(n^2) is preferred over O(n^3) using a numbered list.
gold_points: We usually prefer the tightest upper bound we can justify.
O(n^2) gives more information about the program than the weaker bound O(n^3).
The preferred big-oh expression should be both informative and reasonably simple.
gold_source: Section 3.5 Simplifying Big-Oh Expressions, PDF pages 14-16 (book pages 102-104)
